findings.where: Phone first screen: the order of heading, yellow address strip and the 'I advise…' paragraph inside the hairline frame
findings.fault: On desktop the sentence about what Mark does comes before the address strip, and the strip closes the frame. On phone the strip moves up between the heading and that sentence. The visitor is asked to write to him before being told what he does, and the paragraph left under the strip reads as an afterthought. It also falls below the first phone screen, so that screen gives an opinion and an email address but nothing about what he offers or who it is for.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer opening the site from a LinkedIn link on their phone. Before writing to an advisor they need to know what he advises on and for whom. On phone they meet the request to write first, and must scroll past it to learn why they would.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Download' block (the 'Streamlining the PPP Process' lecture PDF) placed straight under the article's last paragraph
findings.fault: The download sits in the article's own column directly after its closing line, with nothing to separate it. It reads as this article's PDF, but it is a different piece, a 2026 lecture under a 2024 blog post. On desktop the lecture's date and type sit at the far right of the column, apart from its title, which loosens the row further.
findings.who_objects: A reader who wants to keep or forward this article clicks what looks like its PDF and gets a different lecture. Angélique, adding articles, has no pattern showing where an article's own PDF goes and where the list of other papers goes.

findings.where: First screen, desktop and phone: the credential line under the name, 'Formerly Lead Lawyer, PPP Group, World Bank'
findings.fault: This is the page's one piece of proof, and it carries the most weight on the first screen. Yet it is the only line there with no stated source. The footnote at the foot of the sheet sources the hero line as verbatim and marks the supporting line as a draft, but says nothing of this title. The brief bans inventing claims, and a job title close to his real one but not exact is the kind of mistake a procurement reader checks.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who checks his LinkedIn profile against the site. A title that does not match word for word costs trust at first contact. Mark, too, if the title is not one he held.
